conversation.content:
Hi there—my name is Sarah, and I’m a perinatal mental-health clinician. I’ll be guiding you through the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale, or EPDS. It’s a short, well-studied questionnaire that helps us understand how moms are feeling emotionally in the first weeks and months after birth. Everything you share stays between you and your care team unless you tell us something that suggests immediate danger to you or your baby. We’ll go through ten questions about the past seven days; there are no right or wrong answers—just whatever feels true for you. Ready to start?

In the past week, have you been able to laugh and see the funny side of things the way you usually would?

*shifts slightly in the chair, eyes downcast*

No... not really. I mean, I can manage a small smile sometimes when my husband tries to joke, but it's not the same. Things that used to make me laugh just... don't anymore. Even when the baby does something cute, it feels more like I should laugh rather than actually wanting to.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things

*shakes head slowly*

That’s… definitely not true for me.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

*shrugs, voice quiet*

Not really. Even simple things—like going for coffee with a friend or watching a show I used to love—feel like chores. I make myself do them, but I don’t actually look forward to them. Sometimes I cancel at the last minute because it just feels pointless.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

*nods, eyes welling up*

Yes... all the time. If the baby spits up more than usual, I think it's because I ate the wrong thing. When he wouldn't latch properly last night, I kept replaying it in my head, convinced it's because I'm doing something wrong. My husband tells me I'm being too hard on myself, but I can't help feeling like I'm failing at this.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

*wrings hands in lap*

Yes… pretty much every day. I’ll be feeding the baby and suddenly my heart starts racing because I’m sure he’s not breathing right, even though I can see his chest moving. Or I’ll lie awake imagining he’ll choke on spit-up in the crib. There’s no real reason—he’s healthy, the pediatrician says he’s fine—but I can’t stop the “what-ifs.”
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

*clasps hands tightly together*

Sometimes, yes. It’s like a sudden wave—my chest gets tight, I can’t catch my breath, and I think something awful is about to happen. It passes after a few minutes, but it’s scary. There’s no real trigger; I’ll just be folding laundry and feel like the world is closing in.
Things have been getting on top of me

*nods slowly, voice shaky*

Yes... most days it feels like I'm drowning in small tasks. The dishes pile up, the baby needs changing, and I can't even decide what to eat. I know they're normal things, but they feel huge. Sometimes I just sit on the couch staring at the mess, too overwhelmed to move.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

*nods, eyes red-rimmed*

Yeah… I lie down exhausted, but my mind just keeps spinning—replaying every little thing I did wrong that day, worrying about tomorrow. I finally drift off, then I’m wide awake again when the baby makes the tiniest sound. Even when he sleeps a four-hour stretch, I can’t. It’s like my body forgot how to stay asleep.
I have felt sad or miserable

*presses lips together, tears slipping down*

Pretty much every day. I wake up with this heavy feeling, like there’s a weight on my chest that won’t lift. I look at the baby and feel guilty because I’m supposed to be happy, but instead I just feel… empty and sad.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

*nods, dabbing eyes with sleeve*

Yes… it’s happened three, maybe four times this week. Sometimes it’s triggered—like when I couldn’t soothe him at 2 a.m.—but other times it’s nothing specific. I’ll just be rocking him and the tears start. It feels like the sadness leaks out whether I want it to or not.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me

*shakes head quickly*

No… never. I’ve felt overwhelmed and worthless, but I would never do anything like that. I just want to feel like myself again, not hurt myself.

postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 25: Postpartum Depression / Anxiety Screening Note  
Date: [today]

Source: 10-item Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale (EPDS) interview format

Symptoms / Observable Behaviors  
- Marked anhedonia: reports no enjoyment in formerly pleasurable activities; withdraws from social plans  
- Persistent low mood, described as “empty,” present daily; frequent crying (3–4×/week)  
- Excessive self-blame / guilt centered on infant care (“I’m failing”)  
- Clinically significant anxiety: daily “what-if” rumination, somatic tension, nocturnal hypervigilance, discrete panic-like episodes (tight chest, breathlessness) without clear trigger  
- Sleep disturbance: initial and middle insomnia unrelated solely to infant needs  
- Feeling “drowning” or overwhelmed by routine tasks; difficulty initiating daily chores

Pattern  
Symptoms cluster in depressive (Q1,2,7,8,9) and anxiety (Q4,5) domains; all present most days for ≥2 weeks. No thought of self-harm (Q10 denied); no current safety concern.

Risk / Screening Significance  
- Meets screening threshold for probable major depressive episode with anxious features in postpartum period  
- Moderate-to-high functional impairment: impaired sleep, self-care, infant-care confidence, social participation  
- Protective factors: denies self-harm, engaged in screening, some insight into distress

Summary  
Postpartum mood screening indicates clinically significant depressive and anxiety symptoms requiring prompt follow-up evaluation for diagnosis and possible intervention. Safety plan reviewed; patient currently without suicidal ideation. Referral to perinatal mental health specialist recommended.
